options.A: Inspection, auscultation, palpation
options.B: Palpation, auscultation, inspection
options.C: Inspection, palpation, auscultation
options.D: Auscultation, inspection, palpation

explanation: Standard clinical examination dictates looking first, feeling second, and listening with a stethoscope last to gather accurate findings. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T1#BMP125_U2_T1_h3)

question: Why should a pregnant woman be tilted slightly to her side during a physical examination?

options.A: To prevent the heavy uterus from compressing major blood vessels
options.B: To make it easier to measure her height and weight accurately
options.C: To stop her from falling asleep on the examination couch
options.D: To encourage the baby to move into a breech presentation

explanation: Lying flat on the back allows the heavy uterus to press on the main blood vessels, which can lower blood pressure and cause dizziness. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T1#BMP125_U2_T1_h3)

question: What causes the normal first heart sound, known as S1?

options.A: Opening of the aortic and pulmonic valves
options.B: Contraction of the thick ventricular walls
options.C: Closure of the atrioventricular valves
options.D: Blood rushing rapidly into the left atrium

explanation: The S1 sound marks the start of the pumping cycle and happens when the mitral and tricuspid valves snap shut. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T1#BMP125_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which type of heart murmur found during pregnancy is generally considered abnormal and needs a doctor's referral?

options.A: A very soft systolic flow murmur
options.B: Any sound heard with the stethoscope bell
options.C: A loud or diastolic murmur
options.D: Normal splitting of the second heart sound

explanation: While soft flow murmurs are common due to extra blood volume, diastolic murmurs or very loud murmurs always need a closer look. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T1#BMP125_U2_T1_h4)

question: Where is the best place to press when checking for swelling, or pitting edema, in a pregnant woman's leg?

options.A: Over the bony tibia or medial malleolus
options.B: On the soft skin behind the knee joint
options.C: Right in the center of the kneecap bone
options.D: Directly on the soft tissue of the calf muscle

explanation: Pressing against a bone provides a firm surface so you can clearly see how deep an indentation remains after letting go. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T1#BMP125_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which swelling finding is most concerning and requires an immediate check for pre-eclampsia?

options.A: Slight swelling in only one lower leg
options.B: Swelling that affects the face and hands
options.C: Mild swelling around the ankles at night
options.D: Edema that disappears after a short rest

explanation: While mild ankle swelling can happen in normal pregnancy, puffiness in the face and hands is a classic warning sign of high blood pressure disorders. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T1#BMP125_U2_T1_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of doing an electrocardiogram, or ECG, during pregnancy?

options.A: To test the mother's blood sugar and iron levels
options.B: To measure the exact volume of amniotic fluid
options.C: To evaluate the electrical activity of the heart
options.D: To check if the baby has a congenital heart defect

explanation: An ECG records the electrical signals passing through the heart muscle to check its rhythm and overall function. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T1#BMP125_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why can severe anemia put extra stress on a pregnant woman's heart?

options.A: The heart must pump faster and harder to deliver enough oxygen
options.B: Low iron levels cause the heart valves to stick open permanently
options.C: Anemia completely stops the electrical impulses in the heart
options.D: Red blood cells swell up and block the main coronary arteries

explanation: When hemoglobin is low, the blood carries less oxygen, forcing the heart to pump more frequently to make up for the shortage. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T1#BMP125_U2_T1_h6)

question: What specific details should a midwife always write down when recording a heart murmur in a patient's notes?

options.A: The exact brand of the stethoscope used
options.B: Its location and grade or loudness
options.C: The precise weight of the baby in grams
options.D: The name of the manufacturer of the ECG machine

explanation: Noting exactly where the sound is heard best on the chest and how loud it is helps track any changes during future visits. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T1#BMP125_U2_T1_h7)

question: Why is the time right after childbirth a crucial period for watching mothers with heart conditions?

options.A: Large fluid shifts occur as blood returns from the uterus to general circulation
options.B: Breastfeeding stops the heart from beating at a normal regular rhythm
options.C: The mother is usually too tired to notice if she is having chest pain
options.D: Blood pressure drops instantly to zero after the baby is delivered

explanation: After delivery, extra blood flows back into the general circulation from the contracted uterus, which suddenly increases the workload on the heart. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T1#BMP125_U2_T1_h7)

question: What does the top number in a blood pressure reading represent?

options.A: Venous pressure
options.B: Diastolic pressure
options.C: Capillary pressure
options.D: Systolic pressure

explanation: The top number measures the force when the heart contracts, which is known as the systolic pressure. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T2#BMP125_U2_T2_h1)

question: At what threshold is hypertension typically diagnosed in adults?

options.A: 160/100 mmHg or higher
options.B: 100/60 mmHg or higher
options.C: 120/80 mmHg or higher
options.D: 140/90 mmHg or higher

explanation: Persistent blood pressure readings of 140/90 mmHg or higher indicate a diagnosis of hypertension. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T2#BMP125_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which term describes high blood pressure that develops from an underlying medical condition?

options.A: Secondary hypertension
options.B: Primary hypertension
options.C: Idiopathic hypertension
options.D: Essential hypertension

explanation: Secondary hypertension is caused by a known underlying health problem, unlike primary hypertension which has no single clear cause. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T2#BMP125_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which of the following is NOT a modifiable risk factor for hypertension?

options.A: Family history of genetics
options.B: Physical inactivity
options.C: High dietary salt intake
options.D: Excess body weight

explanation: Genetics are inherited traits and cannot be changed, making it a non-modifiable risk factor. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T2#BMP125_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why is hypertension frequently called the "silent killer"?

options.A: It only affects people while they are sleeping
options.B: It often causes no symptoms for a long time
options.C: It causes sudden total hearing loss
options.D: It cannot be detected with a stethoscope

explanation: Many people have high blood pressure without feeling sick, which is why it develops quietly without warning signs. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T2#BMP125_U2_T2_h3)

question: A patient walks into the antenatal clinic complaining of a severe morning headache and blurry vision. What immediate action should the midwife take?

options.A: Check the patient's blood pressure
options.B: Prescribe pain relief tablets
options.C: Send the patient home to rest
options.D: Advise the patient to drink more water

explanation: Headaches and blurry vision combined can signal dangerously high blood pressure or pre-eclampsia, requiring an immediate blood pressure check. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T2#BMP125_U2_T2_h3)

question: What cardiac change commonly occurs when the heart muscle works too hard against high blood pressure over time?

options.A: Atrial shrinkage
options.B: Valvular stenosis
options.C: Myocardial thinning
options.D: Left ventricular hypertrophy

explanation: The heart muscle thickens as it pumps harder against narrowed, high-pressure blood vessels, leading to left ventricular hypertrophy. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T2#BMP125_U2_T2_h4)

question: How does chronic uncontrolled hypertension damage the kidneys?

options.A: By harming the small blood vessels inside the renal tissue
options.B: By causing painful kidney stones to form rapidly
options.C: By blocking the bladder from emptying completely
options.D: By producing excessive amounts of dilute urine daily

explanation: High pressure damages the delicate blood vessels in the kidneys, reducing their ability to filter waste properly. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T2#BMP125_U2_T2_h4)

question: What is a common side effect associated with ACE inhibitors that a nurse should monitor for?

options.A: Severe joint swelling
options.B: Yellowing of the eyes
options.C: A persistent dry cough
options.D: Sudden hair loss

explanation: ACE inhibitors frequently cause a harmless but annoying dry, nagging cough in many patients. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T2#BMP125_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why is medication adherence so important for a patient diagnosed with hypertension?

options.A: Hypertension medications expire within twenty-four hours
options.B: Taking pills irregularly makes blood pressure too low to measure
options.C: Stopping suddenly can cause a dangerous spike in blood pressure
options.D: Missing one pill will instantly cure the condition permanently

explanation: Abruptly stopping blood pressure drugs can lead to a rebound hypertensive crisis, pushing pressure up to dangerous levels. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T2#BMP125_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which dietary adjustment is most commonly recommended to help lower blood pressure?

options.A: Increasing consumption of red meat
options.B: Reducing salt and sodium intake
options.C: Eliminating all forms of protein
options.D: Drinking less clean water daily

explanation: Cutting down on salt helps the body retain less fluid, which lowers the pressure inside blood vessels. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T2#BMP125_U2_T2_h6)

question: A patient with hypertension asks a midwife for advice on exercising safely. What recommendation should the midwife give?

options.A: Engage in moderate physical activity like brisk walking regularly
options.B: Avoid all forms of physical movement to protect the heart
options.C: Lift heavy weights at the gym until complete exhaustion
options.D: Only exercise once a month for several hours at a time

explanation: Regular moderate exercise strengthens the cardiovascular system without placing sudden, dangerous strain on the heart. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T2#BMP125_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the main cause of reduced blood flow to the heart muscle in angina pectoris?

options.A: Atherosclerosis narrowing the coronary arteries
options.B: Excessive production of red blood cells by bone marrow
options.C: Infection and inflammation of the heart valves
options.D: Sudden dilation of the main pulmonary artery

explanation: Plaque buildup inside the coronary arteries restricts blood flow, depriving the heart muscle of necessary oxygen. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why is experiencing angina pectoris an important warning sign for a patient?

options.A: It shows that the patient has completely recovered from heart failure.
options.B: It confirms that permanent death of the heart muscle has already occurred.
options.C: It serves as a warning sign of inadequate oxygen supply to the heart.
options.D: It indicates that the heart is pumping too fast during normal sleep.

explanation: Angina alerts healthcare providers that the heart muscle is stressed and at risk of severe damage if left unmanaged. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h1)

question: Which waste product builds up in the heart muscle when it lacks oxygen, causing pain?

options.A: Potassium bi-urate
options.B: Lactic acid
options.C: Sodium chloride
options.D: Glucose oxidase

explanation: When oxygen is low, the heart switches to a different way of producing energy, which creates lactic acid and irritates local nerve endings. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h2)

question: How does physical activity usually trigger an angina attack?

options.A: It causes the lungs to stop absorbing oxygen from the surrounding air.
options.B: It thickens the blood inside the ventricles to prevent normal circulation.
options.C: It increases the heart rate and workload, raising myocardial oxygen demand beyond supply.
options.D: It instantly closes all major coronary veins and blocks blood return.

explanation: Exercise makes the heart work harder, requiring more oxygen than narrowed coronary arteries can deliver. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which type of angina involves unpredictable pain that can happen even while resting?

options.A: Functional angina
options.B: Stable angina
options.C: Variant angina
options.D: Unstable angina

explanation: Unstable angina occurs without a clear pattern, often at rest, and signals a dangerous worsening of heart disease. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h3)

question: A patient has chest discomfort that always starts after walking two blocks and stops quickly with rest. What type of angina is this?

options.A: Rebound angina
options.B: Stable angina
options.C: Variant angina
options.D: Unstable angina

explanation: Predictable chest pain triggered by a consistent level of activity and relieved by rest points directly to stable angina. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h3)

question: How do patients commonly describe the pain of angina pectoris?

options.A: Heavy pressure or squeezing
options.B: Sharp and knife-like stabbing
options.C: Throbbing localized to one fingertip
options.D: Burning that worsens with swallowing

explanation: Angina is typically felt as a dull, heavy, squeezing pressure across the chest rather than a sharp point. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why might a patient with angina feel pain spreading to the left arm or jaw?

options.A: Nerve signals from the heart share spinal cord pathways with nerves from the arm and jaw.
options.B: The coronary arteries directly connect to the blood vessels of the upper limbs.
options.C: The heart muscle physically stretches outward until it touches the shoulder joint.
options.D: Lactic acid travels rapidly through the lymphatic system into the facial muscles.

explanation: This is called referred pain because sensory fibers from the heart and upper body enter the same segments of the spinal cord. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which diagnostic test uses a special dye to clearly see blockages inside the coronary arteries?

options.A: Standard 12-lead ECG
options.B: Pulmonary function test
options.C: Coronary angiography
options.D: Echocardiogram scan

explanation: Angiography injects dye into the blood vessels of the heart to create clear X-ray images of any narrowing. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h5)

question: Why is a stress test ordered when a patient's resting ECG is completely normal?

options.A: Resting ECG machines are unable to detect electrical signals from the left ventricle.
options.B: Ischemia may only appear on electrical tracings when the heart is working under increased demand.
options.C: It proves that the patient has never experienced any form of plaque buildup.
options.D: It permanently clears any existing blockages from the coronary blood vessels.

explanation: Mild or moderate artery narrowing may not show signs on an ECG until exercise increases the heart's need for oxygen. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is the main way sublingual nitroglycerin helps treat sudden angina?

options.A: Vasodilation to reduce the heart's workload and oxygen demand
options.B: Immediate neutralization of excess stomach acid and gas
options.C: Direct stimulation of the sinoatrial node to speed up heart rate
options.D: Permanent dissolution of large fibrous atherosclerotic plaques

explanation: Nitroglycerin relaxes blood vessels, allowing blood to flow more easily and decreasing the effort the heart must make. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h6)

question: A patient takes one nitroglycerin tablet for chest pain, but the pain does not change after five minutes. What is the correct next step?

options.A: Wait patiently at home for another thirty minutes without medication.
options.B: Engage in light physical exercise to improve overall circulation.
options.C: Take a second tablet and seek emergency medical assistance.
options.D: Take four additional tablets immediately to stop the pain faster.

explanation: Standard protocol involves taking a second dose and getting ready for emergency help if pain continues after five minutes. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the immediate first nursing action when a patient complains of sudden chest pain while walking?

options.A: Document the event in the chart at the end of the shift
options.B: Have the patient stop activity and rest immediately
options.C: Instruct the client to drink a large glass of cold water
options.D: Encourage the patient to walk faster to clear the lungs

explanation: Stopping physical activity right away reduces the heart's oxygen needs and helps ease the lack of blood flow. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why is lifestyle counseling an important part of long-term nursing care for angina?

options.A: It addresses root causes like diet and activity to slow the progression of plaque buildup.
options.B: It completely reverses existing hardened arterial calcium deposits within weeks.
options.C: It eliminates the need for any future medical evaluations or blood tests.
options.D: It guarantees that the patient will never experience another stressful event.

explanation: Healthy eating, regular exercise, and stopping smoking help manage heart disease and slow down the buildup of plaque. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T3#BMP125_U2_T3_h7)

question: What main event causes heart muscle cells to die during a heart attack?

options.A: Severe swelling of the outer heart lining
options.B: Sudden drop in the total volume of body fluids
options.C: Sudden stoppage of blood flow to the heart muscle
options.D: Rapid increase in the resting heart rate

explanation: Cell death happens because a blocked artery cuts off the oxygen supply that the heart muscle needs to survive. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why is a heart attack also called a type of ischaemic heart disease?

options.A: It develops because the lungs fail to filter enough oxygen into blood.
options.B: It results directly from a long-standing infection in the heart valves.
options.C: It only happens when the heart beats too fast during physical rest.
options.D: It is caused by a permanent lack of blood supply to the heart tissue.

explanation: The term ischaemia means a shortage of blood supply, which is the root cause of both chest pain and heart attacks. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h1)

question: How long can blood flow be blocked before permanent heart muscle damage begins?

options.A: 2 to 4 hours
options.B: 20 to 40 minutes
options.C: Exactly 5 seconds
options.D: 12 to 24 hours

explanation: While temporary shortages can recover, true cellular death starts if blood supply is cut off for more than a short window of time. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h2)

question: What change happens inside heart muscle cells right after their blood supply is blocked?

options.A: They begin producing excess proteins to repair the cell wall.
options.B: They stop using glucose and rely entirely on stored body fat.
options.C: They increase their oxygen storage capacity to survive longer.
options.D: They switch from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism, producing lactic acid.

explanation: Without oxygen, cells cannot use normal energy pathways, leading to a buildup of acid that causes pain and damages cell membranes. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which of these is a risk factor for a heart attack that a person can change?

options.A: Biological gender
options.B: Advanced age
options.C: Family history
options.D: Cigarette smoking

explanation: Modifiable risk factors are lifestyle habits or conditions that can be changed or controlled, unlike age or family history. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h3)

question: A patient with narrowed heart arteries does heavy work on a hot afternoon and gets severe chest pain. What most likely caused this?

options.A: A sudden decrease in their normal resting heart rate below normal levels
options.B: An immediate permanent cure of their underlying plaque buildup
options.C: A sudden increase in oxygen demand that the blocked vessel could not supply
options.D: An allergic reaction to the dust raised while working outside

explanation: Heavy physical work forces the heart to work harder and need more oxygen, which triggers ischaemia when arteries are blocked. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h3)

question: How is chest pain during a heart attack typically described?

options.A: A dull ache localized entirely in the right calf
options.B: Crushing or squeezing pressure behind the breastbone
options.C: A mild tickling sensation behind the right ribs
options.D: Sharp, stabbing pain that worsens when breathing in

explanation: Patients usually feel a heavy, tight pressure right behind the breastbone that may spread to the arm or jaw. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why might older adults or people with diabetes feel different or fewer symptoms during a heart attack?

options.A: Differences in nerve pathways and pain perception can mask classic chest discomfort.
options.B: They always have lower blood pressure which prevents any physical pain signals.
options.C: Their coronary arteries never develop complete blockages like younger people.
options.D: Their hearts are completely immune to the effects of sudden oxygen shortage.

explanation: Nerve damage from diabetes or altered nerve responses in older adults often hides the typical crushing pain, leading to atypical presentations. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h4)

question: Within how many minutes of arrival at a clinic or hospital should an ECG be done for a suspected heart attack?

options.A: 2 hours
options.B: 10 minutes
options.C: 60 minutes
options.D: 24 hours

explanation: Speed is critical in heart emergencies, and a fast ECG helps clinicians quickly decide on emergency treatment. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h5)

question: Why are blood tests for cardiac troponins useful in diagnosing a heart attack?

options.A: They measure how much oxygen the lungs are transferring into the blood.
options.B: They are specific proteins released into the blood when heart muscle cells are damaged.
options.C: They show the exact cholesterol level the patient had before the event.
options.D: They calculate the patient's resting heart rate over the past twenty-four hours.

explanation: Troponins stay inside healthy heart cells, so finding them in the bloodstream indicates that heart tissue has suffered injury. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the main reason for giving aspirin right away to someone having a heart attack?

options.A: To permanently cure high blood pressure within minutes
options.B: To lower the patient's body temperature during a fever
options.C: To completely dissolve existing scar tissue in the heart muscle
options.D: To prevent blood cells called platelets from clumping together in the arteries

explanation: Aspirin stops blood cells from sticking together, which keeps the blocking clot from getting larger. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why is opening a blocked heart vessel as fast as possible so important during a severe heart attack?

options.A: It quickly opens the blocked vessel to save starving heart muscle from dying.
options.B: It permanently removes all cholesterol from the entire circulatory system.
options.C: It stops the patient from feeling anxious about being in the hospital.
options.D: It lowers the patient's blood sugar levels back to normal ranges.

explanation: Restoring blood flow quickly limits the size of the heart attack and protects heart pumping function. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the main reason for placing a patient on continuous heart monitoring after a heart attack?

options.A: To assess how well the patient sleeps at night
options.B: To detect dangerous heart rhythm changes early
options.C: To measure the exact amount of daily urine output
options.D: To check the patient's daily blood sugar levels

explanation: Damaged heart muscle is electrically unstable, putting the patient at risk for dangerous rhythm changes that need instant treatment. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h7)

question: Why is careful monitoring of fluid intake and output critical for a patient recovering from a large heart attack?

options.A: Dehydration is the single most common cause of recurrent chest pain.
options.B: A weakened heart pump can easily lead to fluid buildup in the lungs.
options.C: Patients are not allowed to drink water for weeks after the event.
options.D: Kidneys stop working entirely during any routine cardiac episode.

explanation: When the left side of the heart cannot pump effectively, fluid backs up into the lungs, causing breathing difficulties. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common complication following a heart attack?

options.A: Cardiogenic shock
options.B: Heart failure
options.C: Dangerous heart rhythms
options.D: Chronic kidney stone formation

explanation: Kidney stones are unrelated to heart attacks, whereas heart failure, shock, and rhythm problems are classic complications. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h8)

question: What is the main goal of a cardiac rehabilitation program after hospital discharge?

options.A: To ensure the patient never takes any prescribed heart medications again
options.B: To replace all damaged heart valves with artificial mechanical parts
options.C: To completely reverse any existing heart muscle scar tissue back to normal
options.D: To help patients safely rebuild strength and adopt heart-healthy habits

explanation: Cardiac rehab combines supervised exercise, education, and lifestyle guidance to improve recovery and prevent future heart issues. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T4#BMP125_U2_T4_h8)

question: What is the primary physiological problem in heart failure?

options.A: The heart completely stops beating altogether
options.B: The heart rate drops below thirty beats per minute
options.C: The heart muscle fails to pump blood effectively
options.D: The heart valves permanently fuse shut

explanation: Heart failure means the heart pump is inefficient, not that it has stopped beating. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why does fluid backup happen when a patient has heart failure?

options.A: Because patients drink too much water during meals
options.B: Because the kidneys stop producing any urine completely
options.C: Because blood vessels widen and absorb extra fluid from air
options.D: Because the weak heart cannot move blood forward properly

explanation: When the heart cannot pump blood forward efficiently, fluid accumulates behind the failing pump, causing congestion. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which organ triggers the RAAS pathway when blood flow drops in heart failure?

options.A: The kidneys
options.B: The spleen
options.C: The liver
options.D: The pancreas

explanation: Decreased blood flow to the kidneys stimulates them to release renin, kicking off the RAAS cascade. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h2)

question: How does myocardial remodeling eventually affect the heart over time?

options.A: It stops the sympathetic nervous system from working
options.B: It normalizes the blood pressure in all body vessels
options.C: It makes the heart muscle weaker and less efficient
options.D: It cures the underlying muscle damage completely

explanation: While structural remodeling helps temporarily, stretched or thickened heart walls eventually lose their pumping power. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of left-sided heart failure?

options.A: Enlargement of the spleen and pancreas
options.B: Yellow discoloration of the skin and eyes
options.C: Shortness of breath and lung crackles
options.D: Swelling in the lower legs and ankles

explanation: Left-sided failure backs fluid up into the lungs, causing respiratory symptoms like breathlessness and crackles. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h3)

question: A patient presents with severe pitting pedal edema and visible jugular venous distension. Which condition is most likely present?

options.A: Acute bronchial asthma attack
options.B: Severe iron-deficiency anemia
options.C: Isolated left ventricular failure
options.D: Right-sided heart failure

explanation: Systemic venous congestion signs like ankle edema and neck vein distension point directly to right-sided failure. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h3)

question: Which blood test marker is specifically elevated when heart muscle cells are stretched?

options.A: Natriuretic peptides
options.B: Random blood glucose
options.C: White blood cell count
options.D: Serum creatinine levels

explanation: BNP and other natriuretic peptides are released into the blood when ventricular walls experience high stretch and pressure. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of performing an echocardiogram in a patient with suspected heart failure?

options.A: To screen for gestational diabetes during pregnancy
options.B: To check for active bacterial infections in the blood
options.C: To visualize heart structures and measure pumping efficiency
options.D: To measure the electrical rhythm and detect fast heart rates

explanation: An echocardiogram uses ultrasound waves to see heart valves, walls, and calculate the ejection fraction. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is the primary role of diuretic medications in treating heart failure?

options.A: To widen narrowed coronary arteries instantly
options.B: To remove excess fluid and relieve congestion
options.C: To cure underlying heart valve infections
options.D: To speed up a dangerously slow heart rate

explanation: Diuretics help the kidneys eliminate sodium and water, reducing the fluid overload that causes congestion. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why are beta-blockers beneficial for long-term management of heart failure?

options.A: They slow the heart rate and reduce myocardial oxygen demand
options.B: They cause rapid fluid loss through heavy perspiration
options.C: They dissolve blood clots inside the coronary arteries
options.D: They stimulate the kidneys to produce more red blood cells

explanation: By blocking sympathetic stimulation, beta-blockers give the heart muscle a chance to rest and work more efficiently. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h5)

question: What is the most reliable daily indicator of fluid retention in a heart failure patient?

options.A: Daily body weight measurement
options.B: Abdominal girth measurement
options.C: Frequency of bowel movements
options.D: Measurement of daily urine color

explanation: Weighing the patient daily is the most sensitive way to catch early fluid retention before obvious edema appears. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h6)

question: A pregnant woman with heart failure reports severe breathlessness while lying flat in bed. What immediate nursing action should be taken?

options.A: Lay her flat on her back to improve circulation
options.B: Assist her into an upright or semi-Fowler position
options.C: Encourage her to drink a large glass of cold water
options.D: Ask her to perform deep breathing exercises while lying down

explanation: An upright position reduces venous return to the heart, easing lung congestion and relieving orthopnea. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h6)

question: Which specific type of heart failure can develop near the end of pregnancy or postpartum?

options.A: Rheumatic mitral stenosis
options.B: Ischemic heart attack
options.C: Peripartum cardiomyopathy
options.D: Congenital septal defect

explanation: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a unique form of systolic heart failure occurring late in pregnancy or early postpartum. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h7)

question: Why does normal pregnancy pose a serious risk to women with pre-existing heart failure?

options.A: Blood pressure increases to dangerous levels in all women
options.B: The pregnant uterus blocks all blood flow to the lower body
options.C: Kidneys stop filtering waste products during gestation
options.D: Blood volume and cardiac output increase significantly

explanation: The dramatic circulatory expansion of pregnancy forces the heart to pump much harder, which can overwhelm a weak myocardium. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h7)

question: Which dietary adjustment is most important for a patient managing heart failure?

options.A: Eliminating all dietary protein sources
options.B: Avoiding all green leafy vegetables
options.C: Restricting dietary sodium intake
options.D: Increasing daily fluid consumption

explanation: Limiting salt prevents the body from retaining water, which reduces fluid overload and congestion. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h8)

question: Why is teaching patients to recognize early warning signs critical in heart failure care?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for any prescription drugs
options.B: It allows for early treatment before acute decompensation occurs
options.C: It prevents the patient from ever needing an echocardiogram
options.D: It guarantees that heart failure will be permanently cured

explanation: Catching symptoms like sudden weight gain early prevents severe fluid overload that requires emergency hospitalization. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T5#BMP125_U2_T5_h8)

question: Which type of bacteria triggers the immune reaction that can lead to rheumatic heart disease?

options.A: Group A Streptococcus
options.B: Staphylococcus aureus
options.C: Escherichia coli
options.D: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation: Rheumatic heart disease develops as a delayed reaction following an untreated throat infection caused by Group A Streptococcus bacteria. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why do the heart valves get damaged during rheumatic heart disease?

options.A: High blood pressure forces the valves to snap.
options.B: Red blood cells clump together and block tiny blood vessels in the valves.
options.C: Antibodies meant to fight the bacteria mistakenly attack heart valve tissue.
options.D: Bacteria burrow directly into the heart valve tissue.

explanation: The body creates antibodies to fight streptococcal bacteria, but these antibodies mistakenly target similar proteins found in human heart valves. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h1)

question: Which age group is most commonly affected by the initial strep infections that lead to rheumatic fever?

options.A: Infants under one year of age
options.B: School-aged children between 5 and 15 years
options.C: Young adults between 20 and 30 years
options.D: Adults over 65 years

explanation: Children aged 5 to 15 have the highest rates of streptococcal throat infections and are most at risk for acute rheumatic fever. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h2)

question: What is the main reason for giving antibiotics during a strep throat infection?

options.A: To lower body temperature and relieve joint pain
options.B: To instantly repair damage already done to heart valves
options.C: To thin the blood and prevent clots in the heart
options.D: To clear the bacteria and prevent the immune reaction that causes rheumatic fever

explanation: Treating strep throat early with antibiotics clears the bacteria, stopping the immune system from launching an autoimmune attack later. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h2)

question: Which heart valve is damaged most often in rheumatic heart disease?

options.A: Tricuspid valve
options.B: Pulmonary valve
options.C: Mitral valve
options.D: Eustachian valve

explanation: The mitral valve handles high pressure and is statistically the valve most frequently damaged in rheumatic heart disease. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h3)

question: What physical change in the heart valves causes blood to leak backward (regurgitation)?

options.A: The valve cusps fuse together and block all blood flow.
options.B: The valve leaflets become shortened and distorted so they cannot close tightly.
options.C: Calcium turns the valve into solid bone.
options.D: The surrounding heart muscle stretches and pulls the valve wide open.

explanation: Regurgitation happens when scarring warps the valve leaflets, leaving a gap that lets blood leak backward when the heart pumps. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h3)

question: What is a common early sign in a patient developing rheumatic heart disease?

options.A: Shortness of breath during physical activity
options.B: Bleeding gums
options.C: Sudden paralysis of the left arm
options.D: Severe lower back pain

explanation: Shortness of breath during activity is an early warning sign that the heart is struggling to pump efficiently due to valve issues. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h4)

question: A patient with long-term rheumatic heart disease has swollen ankles, an enlarged liver, and raised neck veins. What do these signs suggest?

options.A: Normal pregnancy changes
options.B: Right-sided heart failure
options.C: Mild dehydration
options.D: Acute streptococcal pharyngitis

explanation: Swollen ankles, an enlarged liver, and raised neck veins are classic signs of fluid backup from right-sided heart failure. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h4)

question: Which test is best for confirming structural heart valve damage in rheumatic heart disease?

options.A: Complete blood count
options.B: Echocardiogram with Doppler
options.C: Chest X-ray
options.D: Routine ECG

explanation: An echocardiogram shows real-time images of valve movement, thickness, and blood flow, making it essential for diagnosing this condition. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h5)

question: Why is an electrocardiogram (ECG) often done for a patient with rheumatic heart disease?

options.A: To measure streptococcal antibodies in the blood
options.B: To check for abnormal heart rhythms caused by stretched heart chambers
options.C: To check for bacteria growing on the heart muscle
options.D: To repair torn heart valve tissue with electricity

explanation: Valve problems can stretch the heart's upper chambers, triggering rhythm changes like atrial fibrillation that show up clearly on an ECG. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h5)

question: What is the main medication used to prevent further damage in rheumatic heart disease?

options.A: Heparin injections
options.B: Daily paracetamol tablets
options.C: Benzathine penicillin G injections
options.D: Insulin infusions

explanation: Regular long-term injections of benzathine penicillin G prevent new strep infections and protect the heart from more immune attacks. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h6)

question: What is the main goal of secondary prevention in patients who already have rheumatic heart disease?

options.A: To lower the patient's blood pressure
options.B: To dissolve blood clots in the legs
options.C: To reverse calcium buildup on the valve
options.D: To prevent repeat strep infections and stop further valve scarring

explanation: Prevention stops new strep infections from happening, which avoids extra rounds of inflammation and more damage to the heart valves. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard nursing duty for a patient with established rheumatic heart disease?

options.A: Surgically replacing damaged heart valves in the clinic
options.B: Giving monthly prevention injections on schedule
options.C: Teaching families about treating sore throats early
options.D: Checking the patient for signs of fluid overload and swelling

explanation: Surgical valve replacement is a major operation done by specialized surgeons in an operating theatre, not a routine outpatient nursing task. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h7)

question: A teenager receiving monthly penicillin injections wants to stop because she feels healthy and hates the pain. What is the best response from the nurse?

options.A: Tell her to drink herbal teas instead of getting injections.
options.B: Agree that she can stop taking the medication since her symptoms are gone.
options.C: Explain that regular injections are still needed to protect her heart even when she feels fine.
options.D: Tell her skipping injections only causes mild skin rashes.

explanation: Patients often want to stop treatment when they feel well. Nurses help by patiently explaining that continued coverage prevents silent, ongoing heart damage. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T6#BMP125_U2_T6_h7)

question: Which part of the heart is directly affected by endocarditis?

options.A: The fluid-filled sac around the heart
options.B: The inner lining and heart valves
options.C: The main electrical pacemaker nodes
options.D: The muscular wall of the heart

explanation: Endocarditis targets the endocardium, which includes the inner chambers of the heart and the heart valves. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why is rheumatic heart disease an important risk factor for endocarditis?

options.A: It introduces high levels of fungi directly into the bloodstream
options.B: It completely stops the immune system from fighting infections
options.C: It damages heart valves, making it easy for bacteria to stick
options.D: It permanently weakens the heart muscle contractions

explanation: Previous rheumatic fever scars and damages valve surfaces, providing a rough spot where circulating bacteria can easily attach and grow. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h1)

question: What forms first on an injured heart valve before bacteria attach?

options.A: A hard layer of calcium and scar tissue
options.B: A small clot made of platelets and fibrin
options.C: A collection of white blood cells and pus
options.D: A fluid-filled blister on the valve leaflet

explanation: Initial injury to the heart lining causes platelets and fibrin to gather, creating a small clot that bacteria later stick to. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h2)

question: How do heart valve vegetations protect bacteria from the body's immune system?

options.A: By releasing special chemicals that neutralize antibiotics
options.B: By increasing the body temperature to kill defensive cells
options.C: By surrounding the bacteria with layers of platelets and fibrin
options.D: By pumping white blood cells away from the infected valve

explanation: The layered mass of platelets, fibrin, and multiplying bacteria acts as a shield, preventing immune cells from reaching the microbes. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h2)

question: Which of the following creates a surface that is especially vulnerable to bacterial attachment?

options.A: An artificial prosthetic heart valve
options.B: An enlarged left heart ventricle
options.C: A history of mild hypertension
options.D: A previous episode of viral chest flu

explanation: Prosthetic heart valves are artificial materials that carry a high lifelong risk of bacterial growth and endocarditis. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h3)

question: Why does severe gum disease with bleeding put a person at risk for endocarditis?

options.A: It stops the kidneys from filtering waste products
options.B: It permanently damages the muscular walls of the heart
options.C: It lowers their overall blood pressure dangerously
options.D: It introduces oral bacteria directly into the bloodstream

explanation: Bleeding gums allow normal mouth bacteria to enter the blood vessels during chewing or dental work, traveling straight to the heart valves. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h3)

question: Which classic sign of endocarditis appears as painful nodules on the finger pads?

options.A: Janeway lesions
options.B: Osler nodes
options.C: Roth spots
options.D: Splinter hemorrhages

explanation: Osler nodes are small, tender, raised bumps that appear on the finger and toe pads due to immune complex buildup. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why can diagnosing endocarditis sometimes be delayed in clinical practice?

options.A: It only affects elderly patients who cannot speak about pain
options.B: It never produces a fever during the early stages of the disease
options.C: It causes symptoms that easily mimic common infections like malaria
options.D: It causes immediate and total loss of consciousness in every patient

explanation: Because fever, fatigue, and body weakness happen in many tropical illnesses, endocarditis is frequently mistaken for other routine infections at first. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h4)

question: When should blood cultures be drawn for a patient suspected of having endocarditis?

options.A: Before starting any antimicrobial therapy
options.B: Immediately after the first dose of intravenous antibiotics
options.C: Only after the patient develops a high fever spike
options.D: At the exact time the patient is being discharged

explanation: Blood cultures must be collected before antibiotics are given so that the drugs do not kill the bacteria in the sample, which would cause a false-negative result. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h5)

question: Why is a transesophageal echocardiogram sometimes needed instead of a standard chest ultrasound?

options.A: It safely removes blood clots from inside the heart chambers
options.B: It allows the imaging probe to get much closer to the heart valves
options.C: It measures the exact electrical rhythm of the heart muscle
options.D: It uses radiation to take clear pictures of the lungs and airways

explanation: Passing the ultrasound probe down the food pipe places it right behind the heart, bypassing chest wall tissue to provide a much sharper view of tiny valve growths. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h5)

question: Why must antibiotic treatment for endocarditis be given for several weeks?

options.A: To prevent the patient from developing a drug allergy
options.B: To slowly lower the patient's normal body temperature
options.C: To keep the patient's blood pressure at a stable level
options.D: To penetrate deep inside dense valve vegetations and kill hidden bacteria

explanation: Bacteria tucked inside protective layers of fibrin and platelets require prolonged, high-dose intravenous treatment to be completely cleared. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h6)

question: Which situation would most likely require surgical replacement of a heart valve in an endocarditis patient?

options.A: Severe valve damage causing uncontrollable heart failure
options.B: A single negative blood culture result on the third day
options.C: Mild fatigue and joint pain after walking
options.D: The appearance of tiny splinter hemorrhages under the nails

explanation: When infection destroys valve structures and leads to acute heart failure or other major complications, surgery is required to save the patient's life. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h6)

question: Which physical finding should alert the nurse to potential heart failure in an endocarditis patient?

options.A: Dark lines beneath the fingernail beds
options.B: Small red spots on the palms of the hands
options.C: Crackles or rales in the lung bases
options.D: Painful red bumps on the fingertips

explanation: Fluid backing up into the lungs due to failing heart valves creates crackles or rales, signaling developing heart failure. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h7)

question: What is the primary reason for monitoring intravenous access sites very closely during long-term antibiotic therapy?

options.A: To prevent the development of secondary bacterial infections
options.B: To make sure the patient's blood pressure stays elevated
options.C: To measure the exact amount of urine produced each hour
options.D: To check if the patient is allergic to the plastic tubing

explanation: Long-term IV lines carry a risk of letting new germs enter the bloodstream, which can worsen the patient's infection or cause new complications. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h7)

question: Why is patient education on good personal hygiene and dental care a vital part of preventing endocarditis?

options.A: It keeps the patient's blood sugar levels within a normal range
options.B: It permanently cures any underlying congenital heart defects the patient has
options.C: It stops everyday bacteria from entering the bloodstream through diseased gums or skin
options.D: It replaces the need for surgical heart valve repair in high-risk patients

explanation: Keeping teeth and skin clean minimizes the bacteria that can enter the circulation during daily activities and colonize damaged heart valves. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h8)

question: Which group of patients is most likely to need preventive antibiotics before certain dental procedures?

options.A: Patients with a history of simple high blood pressure
options.B: Patients with artificial prosthetic heart valves
options.C: Patients who recovered from uncomplicated malaria last year
options.D: Patients who experience mild seasonal asthma symptoms

explanation: Individuals with prosthetic valves or previous endocarditis face the highest risk of severe complications, making preventive antibiotics necessary before high-risk procedures. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T7#BMP125_U2_T7_h8)

question: What is the main danger if a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is left untreated?

options.A: It always results in permanent paralysis of the affected limb
options.B: The clot can travel to the lungs and cause a blockage
options.C: The condition automatically triggers severe gestational diabetes
options.D: It causes immediate rupture of major peripheral arteries

explanation: A deep vein thrombosis becomes very dangerous when a piece of the blood clot breaks loose and travels through the bloodstream into the pulmonary arteries in the lungs. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h1)

question: Why does a pregnant woman's body naturally make her blood clot more easily?

options.A: To speed up the overall circulation of maternal blood
options.B: To strengthen the walls of the major deep veins
options.C: To supply extra oxygen directly to the fetal brain
options.D: To prevent postpartum hemorrhage during childbirth

explanation: The body increases clotting factors during pregnancy as a natural protection so the mother can stop bleeding quickly when the placenta separates after birth. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h1)

question: Along with hypercoagulability and blood vessel injury, what is the third part of Virchow's triad that leads to blood clots?

options.A: Venous stasis
options.B: Arterial spasm
options.C: Platelet deficiency
options.D: Cardiac hypertrophy

explanation: Virchow's triad consists of hypercoagulability, blood vessel injury, and venous stasis, which is when blood flow slows down in the veins. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h2)

question: How does the pregnancy hormone progesterone increase the risk of getting a DVT?

options.A: It relaxes smooth muscle and causes venous dilation
options.B: It speeds up the heart rate to dangerous levels
options.C: It directly increases the total platelet count in the blood
options.D: It causes the liver to stop producing clotting factors

explanation: Progesterone relaxes the walls of the blood vessels, making them wider and causing blood to flow more slowly through the legs. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h2)

question: What is the most common sign of a deep vein thrombosis in a leg?

options.A: Unilateral leg swelling and localized tenderness
options.B: Itchy, raised red rashes over both shins
options.C: Symmetrical swelling across both legs equally
options.D: Cold, pale toes with absent pedal pulses

explanation: A DVT usually affects only one leg at a time, causing pain, warmth, and swelling on that specific side. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h3)

question: Why is Homan's sign not a reliable test for checking a DVT on its own?

options.A: It requires expensive laboratory equipment to measure properly
options.B: It is completely unsafe to perform on any pregnant woman
options.C: It can be negative even when a clot is present or positive in healthy patients
options.D: It only works during the first trimester of pregnancy

explanation: Homan's sign is not always accurate. Relying on it alone can lead to missed blood clots or false alarms. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h3)

question: What is the main imaging test used to check for a deep vein thrombosis?

options.A: Complete blood count
options.B: Plain abdominal X-ray
options.C: Compression ultrasound
options.D: Standard electrocardiogram

explanation: Compression ultrasound is a safe, non-invasive scan that clearly shows whether deep veins are open or blocked by a clot. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why is it tricky to interpret a D-dimer blood test in a pregnant woman?

options.A: The test chemicals react negatively with progesterone
options.B: Normal pregnancy naturally elevates D-dimer levels
options.C: Pregnancy completely destroys all fibrin degradation products
options.D: It only works accurately during the first postpartum week

explanation: Because D-dimer levels naturally rise during pregnancy, a positive test result does not automatically mean a woman has a blood clot. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h4)

question: Which medication is generally used to treat a DVT during pregnancy?

options.A: Direct oral anticoagulants
options.B: Intravenous aspirin
options.C: Low molecular weight heparin
options.D: Warfarin sodium tablets

explanation: Low molecular weight heparin is safe to use during pregnancy because its molecules are too large to cross the placenta to the baby. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h5)

question: Why are oral vitamin K antagonist medications avoided in early pregnancy?

options.A: They cause immediate and uncontrollable maternal clotting
options.B: They immediately dissolve all maternal blood platelets
options.C: They stop the placenta from producing any progesterone
options.D: They can cause severe birth defects and fetal abnormalities

explanation: Medications like warfarin can cross the placenta and affect the baby's development, leading to serious birth defects. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h5)

question: What are the classic warning signs of a pulmonary embolism?

options.A: Severe itching across the palms of the hands
options.B: Sudden loss of hearing in both ears
options.C: Sudden shortness of breath and chest pain
options.D: Uncontrollable twitching of facial muscles

explanation: When a blood clot travels to the lungs, it blocks airflow and blood supply, causing sudden trouble breathing and sharp chest pain. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h6)

question: A new mother being treated for a leg DVT suddenly gasps for air, holds her chest, and looks very anxious. What should the midwife do FIRST?

options.A: Report the findings to the doctor immediately as a suspected pulmonary embolism
options.B: Document the mild anxiety in the chart and check her temperature in one hour
options.C: Advise the patient to walk around the ward to improve her general circulation
options.D: Remove her compression stockings and re-measure her calf circumference

explanation: Sudden chest pain and trouble breathing in a patient with a DVT point to a pulmonary embolism, which is a life-threatening emergency needing fast medical help. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h6)

question: What is an important safety instruction for a patient taking blood-thinning medication?

options.A: Stop the medication as soon as leg pain disappears
options.B: Report unusual bruising or bleeding gums immediately
options.C: Take the drug with double doses if a day is missed
options.D: Avoid drinking plain water for two hours after ingestion

explanation: Anticoagulants thin the blood to stop clots, but this also raises the risk of bleeding. Patients must watch for signs of bleeding like easy bruising. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h7)

question: Why are leg exercises and early movement important in postpartum care?

options.A: It completely cures gestational hypertension
options.B: It speeds up the involution of the postpartum uterus
options.C: It encourages muscle movement to prevent venous stasis
options.D: It prevents the development of postpartum breast engorgement

explanation: Moving the legs activates the calf muscles, which pumps blood back up toward the heart and stops blood from pooling in the lower legs. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T8#BMP125_U2_T8_h7)

question: What is the main physical cause of a pulmonary embolism?

options.A: An infection spreading through the airway
options.B: A sudden collapse of the main bronchial tubes
options.C: A severe lack of oxygen in the red blood cells
options.D: A blood clot blocking a vessel in the lungs

explanation: A pulmonary embolism happens when a moving blood clot gets stuck inside the lung blood vessels, blocking blood flow. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h1)

question: Why does pregnancy naturally raise a woman's chance of getting blood clots?

options.A: Red blood cell production completely stops during the third trimester
options.B: The growing uterus permanently damages the valves in deep leg veins
options.C: The body alters clotting factors to prevent heavy bleeding at birth
options.D: Progesterone causes the heart rate to drop significantly at rest

explanation: Pregnancy naturally increases clotting factors so the mother does not bleed too much during delivery. This protective change also raises the risk of unwanted clots. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h1)

question: Where do most blood clots that cause pulmonary embolisms start?

options.A: Small capillaries surrounding the alveoli
options.B: Superficial veins just beneath the skin
options.C: The left chambers of the heart muscle
options.D: Deep veins of the pelvis and lower limbs

explanation: Most pulmonary emboli begin as deep vein blood clots in the legs or pelvis before breaking loose and traveling to the lungs. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h2)

question: What happens in the lungs right after a blood vessel is blocked?

options.A: Oxygen enters the bloodstream without passing through the lung tissue
options.B: Blood rushes into the alveoli and fills the air passages completely
options.C: The entire lung tissue swells up and stops all breathing movements
options.D: Air gets into the lungs, but blood flow to that area stops

explanation: The blockage stops blood from reaching that part of the lung. Air still enters the alveoli, but there is no blood flow to pick up the oxygen. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h2)

question: Which factor is the strongest warning sign that a pregnant woman might develop a pulmonary embolism?

options.A: Carrying a single fetus instead of twins
options.B: Being under twenty years of age at booking
options.C: Having a family history of high blood pressure
options.D: A personal history of past blood clots

explanation: A woman who has had a deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism before is at the highest risk for it to happen again during pregnancy. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h3)

question: Which postnatal patient needs the closest observation for blood clot complications?

options.A: A nineteen-year-old primigravida who walks to the market every morning for exercise
options.B: A thirty-eight-year-old woman with obesity who had an emergency Cesarean section
options.C: A twenty-six-year-old woman recovering normally after an uncomplicated breech birth
options.D: A twenty-two-year-old nursing mother who experienced a quick spontaneous vaginal delivery

explanation: Older age, obesity, and major surgery like a Cesarean section add together to place this client at high risk for blood clots. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h3)

question: What is the most common sign reported by patients experiencing a pulmonary embolism?

options.A: Complete loss of vision in both eyes
options.B: A dull ache radiating down the left arm
options.C: Severe swelling in both ankles and feet
options.D: Sudden and unexplained shortness of breath

explanation: Sudden, unexplained shortness of breath is the main warning sign that should immediately make a nurse think of a pulmonary embolism. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h4)

question: Why do patients with a pulmonary embolism often have a fast heart rate?

options.A: Dehydration from rapid breathing thickens the circulating blood supply
options.B: The clot directly irritates the pacemaker cells inside the heart muscle
options.C: Anxiety from the hospital environment triggers an adrenaline surge
options.D: The heart pumps faster to try and push blood past the lung blockage

explanation: The heart beats faster as a way to maintain enough oxygen delivery when lung blood vessels are blocked. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h4)

question: Which imaging scan is commonly used to clearly see blood flow blockages in the lungs?

options.A: Routine bedside pelvic transvaginal scan
options.B: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
options.C: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography
options.D: Standard abdominal obstetric ultrasound scan

explanation: This specific CT scan uses contrast dye to take pictures that directly show blood clots inside the lung arteries. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h5)

question: Why is a D-dimer blood test harder to interpret in pregnant women suspected of having a pulmonary embolism?

options.A: Normal pregnancy naturally causes D-dimer levels to rise
options.B: Fetal blood cells contaminate the sample and create false lows
options.C: Hormones in pregnancy completely destroy all D-dimer proteins
options.D: The developing placenta blocks the chemical reaction in the test

explanation: Because normal pregnancy is a state where clotting activity is naturally higher, D-dimer levels are already elevated, making the test less reliable for pregnant patients. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h5)

question: What is the immediate first nursing action for a maternity patient showing signs of a sudden pulmonary embolism?

options.A: Encouraging her to walk around the ward slowly
options.B: Placing the woman flat on her back to rest
options.C: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter right away
options.D: Administering high-flow oxygen via a face mask

explanation: Giving high-flow oxygen right away is the critical first step to help correct low blood oxygen levels during a pulmonary embolism. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h6)

question: Why are anticoagulant medications like heparin given quickly to a patient with a pulmonary embolism?

options.A: To instantly dissolve the blockage within two minutes of injection
options.B: To permanently destroy all clotting factors circulating in the blood
options.C: To stop the existing clot from growing larger while the body dissolves it
options.D: To lower the patient's blood pressure and reduce strain on the lungs

explanation: Anticoagulants do not melt clots instantly. Instead, they stop the clot from getting bigger and prevent new ones from forming while the body breaks down the blockage naturally. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h6)

question: Which simple nursing action helps prevent blood clots in the legs for women recovering from childbirth?

options.A: Applying hot water bottles directly to the calves
options.B: Keeping the patient on strict bed rest for a week
options.C: Restricting fluid intake to prevent body swelling
options.D: Encouraging early mobilization and leg exercises

explanation: Getting women moving early and having them do simple leg exercises activates the calf muscles, which pushes blood upward and prevents it from pooling. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h7)

question: Why is drinking enough water important to help prevent blood clots in pregnant clients?

options.A: Water washes away excess clotting factors floating in the bloodstream
options.B: Good hydration stops the leg veins from expanding during pregnancy
options.C: Drinking fluids prevents the placenta from detaching prematurely
options.D: Dehydration thickens the blood, making it more prone to forming clots

explanation: When a person does not drink enough water, blood volume decreases and blood flow slows down, which makes it much easier for clots to form. [learn more](BMP125_U2_T9#BMP125_U2_T9_h7)

question: What is the main reason for taking a gastrointestinal health history?

options.A: To replace the need for physical abdominal examination
options.B: To establish a baseline of normal bowel habits and uncover symptoms
options.C: To calculate the exact caloric intake of the patient
options.D: To diagnose specific surgical emergencies independently

explanation: A health history gathers vital baseline data about normal patterns and current complaints before physical examination. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why is it important to ask about past abdominal surgeries during a GI assessment?

options.A: Prior surgeries guarantee that the patient currently has normal digestion
options.B: Scar tissue from past operations can lead to bowel obstructions or altered pain patterns
options.C: Surgical history has no clinical relevance after the first year
options.D: Abdominal scars prevent the nurse from performing any form of palpation

explanation: Previous surgical procedures often cause adhesions that change anatomical relationships and risk factors for obstruction. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why must you listen to bowel sounds before pressing on the abdomen during an exam?

options.A: Auscultation is the quickest part of the physical check
options.B: Palpation is painful and causes patients to stop the exam
options.C: Listening to the abdomen first warms up the stethoscope
options.D: Palpation can alter natural bowel sounds and peristalsis

explanation: Touching or pressing the abdomen can stimulate bowel motility, creating artificial sounds that do not reflect true baseline activity. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h2)

question: How should you position a patient to make an abdominal examination comfortable?

options.A: Sitting upright with legs dangling over the side of the bed
options.B: Prone with a pillow placed directly under the chest
options.C: Supine with knees slightly flexed to relax abdominal muscles
options.D: Standing upright to allow gravity to pull organs downward

explanation: Flexing the knees relaxes the rectus abdominis muscles, making deep palpation and organ assessment much easier and less painful. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h2)

question: How long must you listen in a single abdominal quadrant before deciding bowel sounds are absent?

options.A: Two minutes per side
options.B: Ten rapid seconds
options.C: Exactly thirty seconds
options.D: A full five minutes

explanation: True absence of bowel activity requires prolonged listening to ensure sluggish sounds are not simply missed. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h3)

question: A patient's abdomen looks very rounded and tight with shiny skin. What is the clinical term for this?

options.A: Abdominal distention
options.B: Symmetrical flat wall
options.C: Scaphoid abdomen
options.D: Normal contour

explanation: Tight, rounded, and shiny skin typically indicates swelling or fluid accumulation known as distention. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is the approximate depth of light palpation during an abdominal check?

options.A: Ten centimeters
options.B: Five centimeters
options.C: Fifteen centimeters
options.D: One centimeter

explanation: Light palpation involves a shallow depression of about one centimeter to check surface texture and superficial tenderness. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of percussing the abdomen?

options.A: To determine if underlying organs contain air, fluid, or solid tissue
options.B: To check for skin temperature variations across different quadrants
options.C: To stimulate sluggish peristalsis in patients with constipation
options.D: To measure the exact blood pressure inside the portal vein

explanation: Percussion produces different tones (like tympany or dullness) that reveal whether underlying structures are hollow or solid. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why do pregnant women often experience frequent heartburn and constipation?

options.A: Growing nutritional needs force the intestines to absorb water much faster
options.B: The enlarging uterus increases stomach acid production significantly
options.C: Elevated progesterone levels relax smooth muscle throughout the gastrointestinal tract
options.D: Decreased blood volume slows down overall systemic circulation

explanation: High progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, slowing digestion and predisposing women to reflux and sluggish bowel movements. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h5)

question: Which factor is NOT a common cause of delayed bowel movements in the early postpartum period?

options.A: Temporary residual smooth muscle relaxation
options.B: Routine daily high-intensity exercise
options.C: Fear of pain around perineal tears or episiotomies
options.D: Painful hemorrhoids making defecation difficult

explanation: New mothers are typically resting rather than performing high-intensity exercise; fear of pain and hemorrhoids are the actual barriers. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h5)

question: What does a test for fecal occult blood primarily screen for?

options.A: Excessive dietary fat malabsorption
options.B: Hidden bleeding within the gastrointestinal tract
options.C: Specific bacterial infections causing diarrhea
options.D: The presence of common intestinal parasites

explanation: Occult blood tests detect microscopic amounts of blood in the stool that are not visible to the naked eye. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h6)

question: Why might a complete blood count be ordered for a patient with a suspected GI problem?

options.A: To measure the exact concentration of digestive enzymes in the stomach
options.B: To determine the primary nutrient absorption rate in the colon
options.C: To check for anemia caused by chronic gastrointestinal blood loss
options.D: To evaluate how fast food moves through the small intestine

explanation: GI bleeding often leads to a drop in hemoglobin and red blood cells, which shows up clearly on a complete blood count. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is a key requirement when documenting gastrointestinal assessment findings?

options.A: Using clear, objective descriptions and standardized medical terminology
options.B: Recording only the patient's subjective complaints without physical data
options.C: Writing all observations exclusively in unstructured personal paragraphs
options.D: Omitting minor details about bowel sounds to save charting space

explanation: Objective and standardized charting prevents miscommunication and ensures safe, continuous patient care. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h7)

question: A postpartum client has a rigid, board-like abdomen and severe pain. What is your immediate priority?

options.A: Report the urgent finding immediately to the attending clinician
options.B: Wait until the end of the shift to document the observation
options.C: Administer a strong oral laxative to relieve potential gas buildup
options.D: Encourage the patient to walk briskly around the ward

explanation: A rigid abdomen is a sign of an acute surgical abdomen or peritonitis, requiring immediate medical evaluation. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T1#BMP125_U3_T1_h7)

question: Which parts of the bowel wall are mainly affected in ulcerative colitis?

options.A: Serosa and adventitia
options.B: Muscularis propria only
options.C: Mucosa and submucosa
options.D: All layers of the bowel wall

explanation: Ulcerative colitis affects the innermost layers of the colon and rectum, specifically the mucosa and submucosa. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T10#BMP125_U3_T10_h1)

question: How does the spread of bowel inflammation in ulcerative colitis differ from Crohn disease?

options.A: Ulcerative colitis is confined strictly to the small intestine
options.B: Ulcerative colitis skips sections of healthy tissue throughout the bowel
options.C: Ulcerative colitis penetrates deeply through the muscle wall
options.D: Ulcerative colitis features continuous inflammation starting in the rectum

explanation: Ulcerative colitis spreads continuously upward from the rectum without leaving skipped healthy patches, which helps clinicians tell it apart from Crohn disease. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T10#BMP125_U3_T10_h1)

question: What is the most common symptom during an ulcerative colitis flare-up?

options.A: Projectile vomiting after meals
options.B: Bloody diarrhea with mucus
options.C: Painful swallowing of food
options.D: Constipation and hard stools

explanation: Because ulcerative colitis creates sores on the inner lining of the colon, bleeding and mucus mixed with loose stool are classic signs. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T10#BMP125_U3_T10_h2)

question: A patient with left-sided colitis will likely feel abdominal discomfort in which area?

options.A: Left lower quadrant
options.B: Right upper quadrant
options.C: Periumbilical area
options.D: Epigastric region

explanation: The descending and sigmoid colon sit in the left lower quadrant, so inflammation there causes cramping and tenderness in that specific area. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T10#BMP125_U3_T10_h2)

question: Which test is considered the main standard for confirming ulcerative colitis?

options.A: Abdominal ultrasound scan
options.B: Colonoscopy with mucosal biopsy
options.C: Barium swallow radiography
options.D: Routine urinalysis and culture

explanation: A colonoscopy allows doctors to look directly at the bowel lining and take small tissue samples to confirm the diagnosis. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T10#BMP125_U3_T10_h3)

question: Why is a stool sample tested when a patient is first evaluated for ulcerative colitis?

options.A: To measure the exact daily caloric absorption
options.B: To test for primary liver enzyme failures
options.C: To confirm the presence of microscopic parasites
options.D: To rule out infectious causes of bloody diarrhea

explanation: Infections can mimic the exact symptoms of inflammatory bowel disease, so doctors check for them before starting long-term treatments. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T10#BMP125_U3_T10_h3)

question: What is the main goal of medical treatment for ulcerative colitis?

options.A: To induce and maintain remission
options.B: To completely eliminate the large bowel
options.C: To permanently cure the genetic defect
options.D: To speed up normal transit time permanently

explanation: Since ulcerative colitis is a long-term condition without a medical cure, treatment focuses on stopping active inflammation and keeping the patient symptom-free. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T10#BMP125_U3_T10_h4)

question: Why are corticosteroids used for short-term relief rather than long-term care in ulcerative colitis?

options.A: They cure the underlying pathology permanently within days
options.B: They completely stop working after the very first week of administration
options.C: They worsen diarrhea instantly if taken for more than a week
options.D: They carry significant risks of adverse side effects with prolonged use

explanation: Long-term steroid use can lead to side effects like bone loss, weight gain, and higher infection risk, so they are not used for continuous maintenance. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T10#BMP125_U3_T10_h4)

question: Which surgery provides a complete cure for ulcerative colitis by removing the affected organs?

options.A: Sigmoid segment resection
options.B: Partial transverse colectomy
options.C: Appendectomy and cecostomy
options.D: Total proctocolectomy

explanation: Removing both the colon and rectum completely eliminates the affected tissue, offering a surgical cure for the disease. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T10#BMP125_U3_T10_h5)

question: What is the main benefit of a J-pouch procedure after a colectomy?

options.A: It preserves normal elimination through the rectum without a permanent bag
options.B: It allows the remaining colon tissue to regenerate new mucosal cells
options.C: It permanently eliminates the need for any follow-up blood tests
options.D: It speeds up the absorption of oral fats in the small intestine

explanation: The J-pouch is an internal reservoir made from the small bowel, letting patients pass stool normally through the anal canal without needing an external stoma bag. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T10#BMP125_U3_T10_h5)

question: During an active ulcerative colitis flare-up, what dietary advice is best to give a patient?

options.A: Increase intake of raw bran and coarse grains
options.B: Consume high amounts of spicy cultural dishes
options.C: Drink plenty of caffeinated drinks for energy
options.D: Avoid high-fiber foods and raw vegetables

explanation: High-fiber foods and raw vegetables can irritate the inflamed bowel lining and worsen cramping during a flare-up. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T10#BMP125_U3_T10_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a primary nursing duty when caring for a patient hospitalized with acute ulcerative colitis?

options.A: Administering prescribed barium contrast studies daily
options.B: Tracking accurate fluid intake and output records
options.C: Monitoring stool frequency and checking for blood loss
options.D: Assessing daily skin integrity and hydration status

explanation: Barium studies are diagnostic imaging tests done occasionally, not a daily nursing task. Monitoring stools, fluids, and hydration are standard ongoing care duties. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T10#BMP125_U3_T10_h6)

question: Which section of the digestive tract can be affected by Crohn's disease?

options.A: Exclusively the stomach and duodenum
options.B: Only the rectum and sigmoid colon
options.C: Any part from the mouth to the anus
options.D: Only the first part of the small intestine

explanation: Crohn's disease can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and often leaves healthy areas in between, unlike other bowel conditions that stay in one fixed spot. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T11#BMP125_U3_T11_h1)

question: Why is recognizing Crohn's disease early so important for patient care?

options.A: It guarantees a complete surgical cure within weeks
options.B: It eliminates the need for any future dietary changes
options.C: It prevents long-term complications like bowel obstruction
options.D: It stops patients from ever needing medication again

explanation: Catching the disease early helps control deep inflammation before it causes permanent scarring, narrowing, and blockages in the intestines. [learn more](BMP125_U3_T11#BMP125_U3_T11_h1)

question: What does the term 'transmural inflammation' mean in Crohn's disease?

options.A: Rapid bacterial infection localized inside the fecal stream
options.B: Inflammation limited strictly to the inner mucosal lining
